title: Heroes Are Not Moral Certificates
subtitle: Two epic openings, two different pressures

learningObjectives.text: What consequence does the Iliad's invocation connect with Achilles' anger?
How does the Odyssey's invocation describe its hero?

ref-iliad-1-opening.author: Homer
ref-iliad-1-opening.excerpt: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans. Many a brave soul did it send hurrying down to Hades, and many a hero did it yield a prey to dogs and vultures, for so were the counsels of Jove fulfilled from the day on which the son of Atreus, king of men, and great Achilles, first fell out with one another.

ref-odyssey-1-opening.author: Homer
ref-odyssey-1-opening.locator: Odyssey 1, invocation and proem; Book 1, normalized characters 0-453
ref-odyssey-1-opening.excerpt: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion;

narrativeBlocks.title: The Iliad names a costly anger
narrativeBlocks.body: The invocation names Achilles' anger and connects it to loss among the Achaeans. It begins with a conflict, not a complete biography of the hero.

narrativeBlocks.title: The Odyssey names an ingenious wanderer
narrativeBlocks.body: Verbatim opening from Samuel Butler's translation: “Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion;”

narrativeBlocks.title: One proem, a different emphasis
narrativeBlocks.body: The Odyssey's opening describes travel, suffering at sea, and the crew's failure to return. The Iliad's opening foregrounds anger and its consequences.

narrativeBlocks.title: Translations are evidence, not the Greek wording
narrativeBlocks.body: These quotations are Samuel Butler's English translations. Keep the work and book locator attached, and do not treat either opening as a universal definition of Greek heroism.

narrativeBlocks.title: Compare the poems, not a single canon
narrativeBlocks.body: The two openings present different narrative problems. Comparison is useful precisely because the poems remain distinct.

quiz.prompt: What consequence does the Iliad's invocation connect with Achilles' anger?

choices.text: A safe return for every crew member
The founding of a unified Athens
Countless ills for the Achaeans and the deaths of heroes

quiz.explanation: The Iliad's opening directly links Achilles' anger with ills for the Achaeans and dead heroes.

quiz.prompt: How does the Odyssey's invocation describe its hero?

choices.text: As a warrior whose anger ends the Trojan War
As an ingenious traveler who suffers while trying to return
As a king who never leaves Ithaca

quiz.explanation: Butler's invocation calls him ingenious, widely travelled, and struggling to save his men and return home.
